title: Gate control: why rubbing helps
objective: Explain how large-fiber input can dampen pain transmission at the dorsal horn.

steps.title: Touch can turn down pain
steps.body: **[[gate control theory|Gate control]]** says activity in large touch ([[Aβ]]) fibers recruits inhibitory interneurons in the [[dorsal horn]] that *reduce* transmission of pain from C fibers. Rubbing a stubbed toe literally dials down the pain signal before it ascends.

flag.note: The original 1965 circuit is a simplification; the real interneuron wiring is more complex, but the core 'touch gates pain' idea holds.

steps.setup: You bang your elbow and immediately rub it.
steps.prompt: In gate-control terms, why does rubbing ease the pain?
options: Aβ touch input recruits inhibition that dampens the pain signal
Aβ input directly silences the C-fiber endings out in the skin
Rubbing spreads inflammatory chemicals away from the injury
Rubbing cools the skin below the pain threshold for a while
steps.reveal: The touch input engages inhibitory interneurons that 'close the gate' on C-fiber pain transmission in the dorsal horn — a central effect, not destruction of nociceptors.

variants.prompt: Rubbing a painful spot helps mainly because…
options: Touch input recruits dorsal-horn inhibition of pain
Touch fibers silence the pain endings out in the skin
It washes pain chemicals away from the injured spot
variants.explanation: Large-fiber touch input gates C-fiber pain transmission centrally.

steps.prompt: Gate control is the principle behind which everyday device?
options: A TENS unit that stimulates nerves to relieve pain
A heating pad that gently warms up sore muscles
An ice pack that numbs the area around an injury
A numbing cream that blocks nerve signals in the skin
steps.explanation: TENS drives large sensory fibers to engage the inhibitory gate, damping pain — a direct application of the theory. Heat and ice work by other mechanisms.

variants.setup: A device delivers mild electrical stimulation to sensory nerves for pain relief.
variants.reveal: TENS recruits large-fiber input to gate pain transmission.

reviewNotes: Gate control, with the simplification flagged.
